problem: Learned neural navigation policies (mostly RL) are trained in simulators that lack either real-world visuals or robot physics, so they rarely deploy on real robots at long range. Prior real-image environments are too small or sparsely captured, or they rely on a human operator to execute actions.
motivation: Simulators rarely provide both visual realism and accurate robot dynamics, so a single-policy sim-to-real transfer is hard. Splitting the policy into a high-level planner trained on real images of the deployment site and a low-level controller trained on simple synthetic physics lets each use a cheap environment suited to it.
key_idea: A two-level policy: a high-level RGB planner trained by imitation on a street-view-like image graph of the deployment building, and a low-level 1D-LiDAR controller trained with DDPG in a synthetic maze. Together they navigate long range on a real robot.
insight: Separating visual/layout knowledge from physical control allows each to be trained in a cheap, appropriate environment and still deploy directly on a real robot. Ablations show that more traversals help (1 traversal 0.75 vs 2 or 3 at 0.96), and that image goals are ambiguous (0.85, rising to 0.89 with an extra opposite-direction view). The learned low-level policy beats a ROS local planner (9/10 vs 6/10 runs), and human demonstrations induce socially aware paths that avoid cubicle areas.
method: High-level policy: ResNet50 (ImageNet pretrained) image embedding + proximity bit + MLP goal embedding fed into a single-layer LSTM (dim 2048). It outputs a progress value for each of forward / turn left / turn right, and the action is the argmax.
Goal specification: a one-hot label over a 10x10 grid (77 valid cells) or an embedding of a target image from the same network.

Image-graph environment: a 6-camera hexagonal rig captures panoramas every 0.5 m, stitched and cropped into 24 views 15° apart (108x90° fov). Cartographer poses define forward (about 1 m, valid if an image lies within 0.7 m) and 15° turns.

High-level training: imitation of shortest-path or human-demonstration paths with a squared loss on progress y = d(x,g) - d(x',g). It uses DAgger-like on-policy unrolls in a distributed setup (200 collectors, 5 trainers, unroll length 40, batch 8, lr 1e-4).

Low-level policy: a ConvNet over the last 3 1D LiDAR readings stacked as an image (conv-conv-fc20-fc10) outputting continuous differential-drive wheel velocities. It executes 'forward' while staying straight and safe.
Low-level training: DDPG in a synthetic 2D-extruded hallway/room maze with simulated diff-drive kinematics. The reward is 1.0*v_lin - 0.8*|v_ang|, with -1.0 on collision (following Chiang et al.).
Human demonstrations: 70 labeled human paths to one target supervise the planner, yielding socially aware behavior.

setting.backbone: ResNet50 + LSTM high-level policy (trained); ConvNet low-level policy (DDPG, trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Panorama scans of a 200m x 100m office building (3 traversals, images every 0.5 m, 24 views per location) with shortest-path supervision; the low-level policy is trained in a synthetic maze simulator.
setting.observation: Monocular RGB (high level) + proximity bit + 1D LiDAR (low level, last 3 readings)
setting.action_space: High level: discrete forward ~1 m / turn left / turn right 15°; low level: continuous differential-drive wheel velocities
setting.simulator: Custom real-image graph environment (panorama scan of the building) + synthetic 2D-extruded maze; real Fetch robot
setting.privileged: Pre-exploration: the deployment building is scanned in advance to build the image graph with Cartographer poses; no map or localization is needed at test time.

numbers.eval_set_note: 200 runs: 10 targets x 20 random starts at least 30 m away, on a holdout traversal
numbers.method: High-level policy (location label goal, shortest-path supervision, 3 training traversals)
numbers.extra: Trained on the same building's earlier scans; success = within 3 m of target
numbers.evidence: The high level policy achieves near perfect success rate of 0.96 on the test traversal.

numbers.extra: Target given as a random image from the target area; with an additional opposite-view image SR=89
numbers.evidence: Using this setup, we achieve 0.85 success rate.

numbers.eval_set_note: 10 targets x 4 runs = 40 runs, no manual intervention
numbers.extra: Real Fetch robot; success within 3 m; ROS Navigation Stack baseline gets 0.75
numbers.evidence: achieves success rate of 0.80 over these 40 runs

numbers_note: Only success rate is reported (no SPL/NE). Average run length is 1.24x the shortest path and about 78 steps.
results: On a real Fetch robot in a 200m x 100m office building, the method reaches 0.80 SR over 40 long runs, beating the ROS Navigation Stack (0.75) while needing less setup and no manual localization. In the image-graph test it reaches 0.96 SR, and the learned low-level policy succeeds in 9/10 runs vs 6/10 for a ROS local planner.
limitations: Requires a per-environment scan and retraining for each new deployment, and it is sensitive to environmental changes (moved furniture) and to areas missing from the scan.
Small real-robot evaluation (40 runs, one building); failures include leaving the trained area and low-level collisions; the ROS baseline comparison is modest (0.80 vs 0.75).
Image-goal specification is ambiguous in repetitive environments (0.85 SR).
builds_on: Mousavian et al. 2018 (Visual Representations for Semantic Target Driven Navigation)
Chiang et al. 2018 (Learning Navigation Behaviors End-to-End)
compares_to: ROS local planner as low-level replacement
